item.title: Able to Bend, Not Break
item.description:
Parenting

Able to Bend, Not Break

Raising resilient kids in a culture of achievement.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • High-achieving youth are now considered an at-risk group for anxiety, depression, and substance use.
  • Distress rises when children believe their self-worth depends on performance or achievement.
  • Research finds that resilience is built through relationships and ordinary rituals and routines.
  • Parents can promote a child's resilience by highlighting more than just the outcomes.
Source: Vitolda Klein/Unsplash

Elite travel teams, private coaching, and exceptional academic performance were once reserved for a few extraordinary students or athletes. For today’s middle- and upper-middle-class families, these pursuits have become the norm. Yet the children striving to excel amid this intensity are struggling. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2019) identified high-achieving youth as one of the most at-risk groups for anxiety, depression, and substance use, alongside youth exposed to deep poverty, trauma, and discrimination. Children with every apparent advantage have converged on the same risk profile as those we traditionally identify as most vulnerable.

Achievement culture—a social environment that prizes goal attainment, exceptional performance, and external accomplishment—is fueled, in part, by a fear that children will fall behind if these pursuits are neglected. Today, it has become ambient and nearly impossible for young people to escape. Social media amplifies constant comparison, competition for college admission continues to intensify, and pressure from adults reaches children even in families that deliberately emphasize effort, character, and well-being. Parents do not have to embrace achievement culture for their children to absorb its messages.

On Resilience, Ambition, Passion and Gifted Children

Striving for excellence and developing one's potential are worthy goals. And, parents may ask, what about the exceptionally gifted child, or the child with a fierce passion for a pursuit who is driven to grow? Ambition and high expectations are not the problem. The harm emerges when children begin to believe their worth depends on what they achieve.

Research by Suniya Luthar and colleagues in high-achieving schools has consistently found elevated rates of anxiety, depression, and substance use. A key driver is that many students come to perceive their self-worth as contingent upon performance. Distress is further amplified by parental criticism, perceived parental values that prioritize achievement over character, competitive peer relationships, and negative social comparison.

The intersection of high-achieving schools, affluence, and perfectionism may be tricky to disentangle. As a broad generalization, high-achieving schools are associated with an environment where an emphasis on outcomes may drive students to adopt perfectionist traits, and these schools may also be populated by affluent kids who have the resources to gain a competitive edge through tutors, elite athletic clubs, or coaches who drive improvement. Research on what protects young people from the excesses of achievement culture points in a surprising direction: not toward better strategies for succeeding, but toward stronger relationships.

Luthar summarizes decades of research with a simple conclusion: "Resilience rests, fundamentally, on relationships." The evidence extends well beyond high-achieving schools. In a statewide study of positive childhood experiences, Bethell and colleagues found that every protective experience associated with better adult mental health was relational: being able to talk with family about feelings, feeling supported by friends, having trusted adults outside the home, feeling safe at home, belonging at school, and participating in community traditions. Adults who reported the highest number of these positive childhood experiences had dramatically lower odds of depression and poor mental health than those who reported the fewest.

Resilience researcher Ann Masten offers a useful reframe. What protects children is often not extraordinary at all, but what she calls the "short list" of ordinary magic: a stable, caring adult, a school and community where a child is truly known, and routines and rituals that foster belonging and a positive sense of identity.

Source: Veronica Elmore/Unsplash

Building Resilience

If resilience is the ability to adapt, recover, and continue growing through adversity, the evidence suggests it is built through ordinary, repeatable practices and relationships, rather than extraordinary interventions. The list below offers parents a starting point for building or augmenting a culture of resilience at home.

Separate worth from achievement. Praise effort, curiosity, persistence, character, adaptability, and growth—not just outcomes. For those gifted and accomplished scholars, athletes, and artists, take interest in their achievements, of course. And, make an effort to balance encouragement and validation while acknowledging that a child is more than their gifts or accolades. Gordon Flett’s (2025) book Mattering as a Core Need in Children and Adolescents: Theoretical, Clinical, and Research Perspectives summarizes literature on being valued and needed by others, which contributes to a youth’s sense of well-being and resilience.

Change the first question. What you ask after school, after the game, or after the test is one of the clearest signals of what you value. Lead with the child before the outcome: "How are you?" or "Who did you eat lunch with?" before "How did it go?”

Recruit other caring adults. Some of the strongest protective relationships are with adults who are not parents. Cultivate and nurture relationships a child may have with coaches, teachers, relatives, neighbors, or mentors; adults who know your child for who they are, not simply for what they accomplish.

Protect ordinary rituals. Family dinners, traditions, and unstructured time are not what remains after practices and tutoring; they are among the very experiences that foster resilience.

Expand your family's tolerance for failure. Modeling from adult behavior is one of the leading ways children learn. Talk openly about your own setbacks and how you recovered from them. Parents who treat failure as an opportunity to learn, rather than something alarming, raise children with more adaptive mindsets.

Tend to your own relationships. Parents who experience unconditional acceptance and dependable support in their own lives impact their parenting quality and perceived parenting stress. Your friendships and sources of connection are not indulgences; rather, they are part of your child's resilience infrastructure.

Resilience in children is not a genetic trait they are born with or without. Resilience is built through everyday relationships and experiences. When children know their worth is intact, no matter the outcome, they get better at bending without breaking.

item.title: The Country You’re Angry at Is Partly Imagined
item.description:
Behavioral Economics

The Country You’re Angry at Is Partly Imagined

Political division grows when we mistake imagined extremes for real ones.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • We picture the other side as more extreme and more united than it is. We get our own side wrong too.
  • Believing there is only one right answer makes us less tolerant. Most of us recognize that pluralism exists.
  • The perception gap is a mistake, not a real disagreement. That makes it the easier one to close

Two people describe the same politician. One writes, “A disgusting monster destroying America.” The other writes, “I disagree with his policies.” Give them a policy survey and their answers look almost identical: taxes, immigration, health care, all broadly similar. What differs is not the belief, but the volume.

Much of what looks like division is volume. And even within a single party, people agree far less than they think.

The referee stops calling fouls

Picture a referee at a game between two rival teams. As long as he stays neutral, both sides play straighter, because nobody wants to foul in front of a fair judge. Now let the referee pick a side. He does not stop blowing the whistle. He stops blowing it for the same fouls.

This is consistent with what we found with 2,400 Americans. Some people divided $10 between two strangers, one who loved Trump and one who opposed him, while keeping none of it for themselves. A bystander could then judge their behavior and dock their bonus for the split. When bystanders broadly agreed on what was fair, the even split drew the least punishment, while the most lopsided split drew the most. Once the crowd polarized, that discipline broke down. A partisan bystander punished a clean 50-50 split about as much as a fair-minded one punished a split that gave everything to one side. So the splits became about 50 percent more lopsided than they were in front of a fair-minded crowd.

The more divided the crowd, the less fairly people allocate resources
Source: My simplified redraw of Dimant et al. (2025) - Divided We Act

The main takeaway here is that the existing division is not solely driven by idiosyncratic preferences for polarization but is also shaped and amplified by the (anticipated) polarization around us. Whether this impression is correct, and what to do about it if not, is a core consideration that I am going to turn to next.

We imagine a more extreme country than the one we live in

Why would a referee stop calling fouls? Because polarization runs on a story we tell ourselves about the other side, and that story is often wrong. Think of the coworker you were sure had voted the other way, the one you assumed thought you were a fool. Then you finally compared notes and agreed on four things out of five. You had just been shouting about the fifth, the one that disunites you.

That misperception has a name: the perception gap. Based on existing research, Democrats and Republicans each believe that about 55 percent of their opponents' views are extreme. However, the real figure is about 30. The most politically engaged hold the most distorted picture of all, and across more than thirty years of survey data, perceived disagreement consistently outruns the real thing.

It does damage, because hostility feeds on what we expect of the other side. In my own work, when people cooperated less with the other party, it was not because they were unwilling. In fact, they were willing to an almost surprising degree. They just wrongly assumed the other side was not and would potentially screw them over. People brace for a hostility that never comes.

Even the sense of a lawless opposition is partly a mirage. Across the political spectrum, Americans condemn violations of core democratic rules, such as refusing to accept an election result. What they cannot agree on is how bad each violation is. They do not think their neighbors are secretly anti-democratic. They think their neighbors are all over the map, so nobody knows who will object when a rule is broken.

Even the other side is not one side

If the gap between the parties is partly imagined, the gap inside a party is stranger still. It is not just that the other party contains multitudes. Yours does too. Picture your family talking through immigration over dinner: one person wants the border sealed, another wants a path to citizenship, and a third just wants the paperwork to work. Same politics, three different people.

A study of almost 1,000 politically representative Americans asked not only what people believe, but what they think everyone else believes. The findings suggest that even on immigration, we do not picture two camps. The three views we imagine to be most common in the country are held, we guess, by only 21, 14, and 12 percent of us. And we cannot even map our own side very well. Asked to sketch the spread of opinion within their own party, Democrats agreed with each other about a quarter of the time. Republicans agreed about a third.

One takeaway is that consensus is much less frequent than we tend to believe, even on issues with high visibility. This, in turn, amplifies our societal division.

Believing there is only one right answer makes us harsher

Most of us still act as if there were one. That is what is responsible for the existing polarization.

In other work, we gave people real money to divide and let bystanders punish how it was divided. When we forced bystanders to name a single acceptable way to split the money, punishment was 64 percent. When we allowed them to name several acceptable ways, it fell to 45 percent. A control group, never prompted about norms, sat at 54 percent. Naming one right answer made people harsher. Considering that there are several made them gentler, by about nine points in each direction.

Left to themselves, people recognized four or five different norms in the same situation. Only about one in seven insisted on just one. And once you are sure there is only one right answer, anyone who acts differently is not offering an alternative. They are simply wrong. Wrong is easier to punish than different.

See one 'right answer' and you punish more
Source: My simplified redraw of Panizza et al. (2025) - Pluralism breeds tolerance

What the words give away

Believing in one right answer licenses the punishment. Read what people write, and you can pick out who will use it.

I went back to what people wrote about Donald Trump, some in loathing and some in devotion, written in private, before they ever faced an opponent. It turns out, the way we use divisive language predicts our discriminatory tendencies well. But language is nuanced, and so are the ways in which it predicts actual behaviors.

Political language was not a general marker of selfishness. Text written before participants knew their partner’s politics became informative only when a meaningful partisan divide entered the decision: hostility marked people who expected less from opponents and therefore cooperated less, while writing in absolutes marked people who penalized opponents even when expectations could not matter. These two tendencies barely overlapped, so partisan discrimination is not one problem with one remedy. In the reported experiments, nudges reduced the belief-driven penalty only among the most hostile writers, had no average effect, and left the conviction-driven penalty untouched.

The country you are angry at

The solution is not to pretend the disagreement away. Some of it is real, and some of it runs deep. The solution is to get specific about where it actually lives, because the imagined version is what makes the harshness feel justified. A person who disagrees with you becomes a person who must be wrong, and wrong is what gets punished. Before you decide your opponents think with one voice, remember that they almost never do. Neither do you.

The country you are angry at is, in good part, one you imagined. So, before you blow the whistle, check whether you are calling a foul or just checking a jersey.

item.title: 4 Reasons the Workplace Isn't Designed for Our Brains
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

4 Reasons the Workplace Isn't Designed for Our Brains

Small shifts in how we work can help protect our focus, energy, and performance.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Many workplaces are designed for output, but don't align with the way human brains naturally work.
  • Multitasking reduces focus and increases cognitive load.
  • Small changes in work habits can improve focus, well-being, and performance.
Source: Sree Mitra / Used With Permission

Humans aren’t machines. We have emotions, relationships, creativity, and needs that can’t be measured like a machine’s output. Yet many workplaces are designed as if we function the same way.

Modern offices often assume that placing people in a factory-like environment will produce factory-like results. When we struggle with focus, feel drained, or fall behind, we often blame ourselves, even when our environment is contributing to the problem.

I recently spoke with Sree Mitra, founder and CEO of Q Studio, a leading expert in workplace performance, cognitive skills development, and helping individuals and organizations adapt to the demands of the modern work environment. Through her “Mind Skills” approach, Mitra helps high-performing professionals navigate pressure, adapt to change, and perform at their best. She explains why many modern workplaces conflict with the way our brains are designed to work.

1. The Brain Switches, It Doesn't Multitask

Most workplaces involve a lot of multitasking. For instance, an average office worker might go from answering a phone call about a new project, to updating status on another project, to building a presentation about a third project. This actively works against the way your brain wants to function.

Multitasking takes a significant toll on the brain's ability to focus; each focus switch leaves what one paper calls "attention residue," where cognitive activity about the previous task persists into the new one. This saps the brain's resources.

"The key to productivity is being able to focus on one thing at a time," says Mitra. "Concentration can be trained; you can create conditions that make it easier. When people learn to work in long, uninterrupted blocks of time instead of reacting to every notification, their productivity actually grows over time."

2. Open-Plan Offices May Cause Overload

Many modern offices have moved to open floor plans. Open-plan offices feel like they should be the best option; they make the space feel bigger, and common wisdom says that when you remove barriers between people, they're more likely to interact.

Unfortunately, the evidence doesn't support this. In fact, it states the opposite. Research shows that open-plan offices decrease face-to-face interaction by up to 70% and force more digital communication, and productivity dips.

There's a cognitive load that comes with existing in the same space as a lot of other people, and even something as minor as a cubicle wall can help ease that load. Removing it may feel better from a management perspective, but it doesn't actually work.

3. The Eight-Hour Workday Isn't Really Eight Hours

The eight-hour workday has been a standard for many decades, thanks to labor unions and legislation. A 15-minute break in the morning, a 15-minute break in the afternoon, and a half-hour or hour for lunch is a normal expectation. But this rigid structure doesn't allow for the way our brain works.

The standard workday assumes that people can hold steady focus on a task for hours, but after sustained attention for a long enough period, that focus naturally begins to decline. Literature shows that taking micro-breaks and stepping away from a task for a brief break resets focus and restores energy. Without the flexibility to do this, workers risk burnout.

"When you never let your mind reset, you create cognitive overload," says Mitra. "The brain regulates its focus, emotion, and decision-making in cycles. If you're constantly forcing it to run at top speed, your decision-making and the quality of your work suffers."

4. The Need to Always Be Connected

"Have you tried turning it off and on again?" is more than a computer troubleshooting tip. When a computer goes for a long time without restarting, temporary data builds up, maintenance tasks and updates go undone, and small errors begin to compound. The same is true of the human brain.

With email, instant messaging, and smartphones, work can follow us anywhere, even beyond the workday. There's a constant low-grade stress that comes with increased connectivity. Minimizing your off-the-clock availability for work messages lets your brain "restart" and do upkeep, consolidating memory and fueling creativity.

Action Steps

You can't redesign the office, but you can change how you work within it.

  • Protect your focus: Create blocks of uninterrupted time for important work, and limit distractions when you need deeper concentration.
  • Take short resets: Your attention isn't unlimited. Step away every 60 to 90 minutes, even briefly, to recharge before your energy drops.
  • Create boundaries: Open offices make it easy for work to follow you everywhere. Use headphones, a quiet space, or clear signals with your team to protect your focus.
  • Set a stopping point: Your brain needs time away from work to recover. Decide when you're done for the day, and protect that time.
  • Get outside when you can: A short walk between meetings, a few minutes in the sun at lunch, or a call taken outdoors can restore attention that hours indoors wear down.

The Bottom Line

Most of us can’t escape office life, but we don’t have to blame ourselves for struggling in environments that weren’t built with the brain in mind. However, small changes in how we work, recharge, and create boundaries can help us feel more focused, energized, and in control.

item.title: Lessons from Dog Training When Life Feels Hopeless
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Lessons from Dog Training When Life Feels Hopeless

Personal Perspective: Regression, though temporary, can disguise progress.

Posted July 15, 2026

Source: Tracy Strauss

There are days when life feels hopeless. But the feeling of hopelessness and factual hopelessness are not necessarily the same thing.

My dog Beau’s separation anxiety is a fact: A clinical medical condition. It took a few years of desensitization training and medication for him to feel calm staying home solo.

There were many days when his condition felt hopeless. In the beginning, he couldn’t tolerate three seconds alone without a full-blown panic attack: barking, hyperventilating, and self-destructive behaviors. A behavioral trainer told me there was hope: I could change Beau’s mindset and behavior. I could leave home freely.

There wasn’t a definite timeframe for this change, but it could be weeks or months. Over weeks and months, Beau progressed to a few minutes solo and then regressed. We had to begin the desensitization training over. This pattern repeated.

The trainer explained that regressions were a normal part of the process, but when we lost what we worked hard to gain, over and over, I began to feel hopeless. When months of training turned into a year, then two, my feeling of hopelessness grew.

The Dark Days of Hopelessness Don't Last

Why did I keep going? I asked myself this every time Beau regressed. What was stronger than my hopelessness was a hope-laden bedrock that told me not to give up. When a vet told me Beau would never be a dog who could stay home for four hours, I felt defiant. How did she know? And yet she was the expert, so perhaps I was in denial. Perhaps I should have accepted the truth as the vet presented it.

But there were factors other than Beau’s medical condition; he was attacked at his daycare and then on the street. We lived in a neighborhood where police sirens circled our neighborhood dozens of times a day, and where stepping outside into the bombardment of scooters, skateboarders, and gang violence scared Beau. I told myself these factors, and not the facts of his condition, were what caused problems for his progress.

As a human being with complex PTSD, I understood how difficult changing a habit rooted in survival panic could be. At the same time, I debated whether I was a good dog parent. Maybe Beau would’ve lived a happier life with somebody else. Maybe he wouldn't be so anxious. I spun a story that I was the problem.

Source: Tracy Strauss

Change the Story

The stories we tell ourselves can cause more harm than good. Many times, such stories are filled with assumptions, biases, and the past. For me, the story was rooted in what I’d gleaned as a child growing up in an abusive home: I didn’t deserve love. I didn’t deserve a dog. And if I dared to defy this decree, I’d be punished. The fact was, I’d ended up with a special dog, one who had special needs.

Four years later, Beau stayed home for four hours, relaxing. The vet’s prognosis for Beau hadn’t been a fact, only a hopeless opinion.

Setbacks Aren't Endings

Recently, we moved. Within three weeks, we made our way to a one-hour solo time, something that previously took years to attain. And then, suddenly, Beau was unable to tolerate five minutes alone. He rushed the door, then barked when I left, and escalated to hyperventilation. It had been two years since his last regression.

I’d thought he was cured. Now, I thought my hopefulness had been hubris.

I wracked my brain for a reason for the regression: Was it the landlady’s intrusions with workmen that caused his anxiety to resurge? Are the smoke alarms malfunctioning?

I was housebound again and devastated. Instead of thinking of the setback as temporary, I assumed it was forever.

A cognitive bias is an error in thinking that affects how we perceive situations. We might think of a bias as the “story” we tell ourselves about an interaction, an event, or a person; we rely upon our “story” as “fact,” which can lead us down a path of unnecessary suffering.

Finding myself a prisoner to Beau's separation anxiety again, I assessed my new situation based on a past scenario: I’d been wrong to think I could cure Beau of his separation anxiety. I drew upon an old childhood belief: if I tried to leave that terrible home, bad things would happen. Leaving, like staying, was hopeless.

Last night, I wept over my dinner plate. Unable to eat, I told myself to face the fact: my fate was to be trapped with this terrible anxiety. How dare I think differently? The fact was, I felt hopeless. But feelings aren’t permanent. And making an assumption about the future based upon a feeling or a bias doesn’t change the future, or the present, or the past—it only creates suffering.

I didn’t know how Beau would do the next day or after. I had a choice: to assume he would do poorly or to believe in other possibilities. The fact was, nothing about the future was yet a fact.

Source: Tracy Strauss

Choose to Think Differently

When you find yourself trapped in a hopeless loop, there are practical things you can do to cultivate relief: breathwork, cognitive reframing, and pleasure-seeking activities.

I knew today that I wasn't going anywhere by myself, so I put Beau in the car and drove us to his favorite place, a peninsula with rolling hills and the Massachusetts Bay. We hadn’t gone there in more than eight months; back in the day of Beau’s severest separation anxiety, we used to go weekly, and then, perhaps a coincidence or perhaps as a result, his anxiety eased. When we were a few blocks from our destination, Beau stuck his head out the window and squealed. For the next hour, we forgot about everything. We immersed ourselves in this beautiful place, where joy prevailed.

The next time hopelessness prevails, call upon doggedness to be your beacon.

item.title: Aesthetic Connection in the Digital Age
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Aesthetic Connection in the Digital Age

Personal Perspective: Is capturing live music on our phones really experiencing it?

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Shared music experiences are dynamic.
  • When we experience music there is a connection between the music source and ourselves.
  • Live music experiences should be a pure form of aesthetic exchange where one is experiencing the moment.

Shared music experiences are dynamic. Or at least they are supposed to be. When we experience music, there is a connection between the music source and ourselves. This is especially true in "live" music experiences. There is interaction between the one providing the music and the one receiving it. The audience is just as important as the performer, with energy going back and forth. The performer thrives on the energy from the audience and, in return, the audience experiences a full mind, body, and soul aesthetic experience.

Any musician will tell you that they are "fueled" by the audience; not just the response of applause but the feeling and connection that the music creates between both entities. The musician and the audience are in concert (pun intended) with each other within the aesthetic experience.

Source: ChiccoDodiFC / iStock

I’m sure you can recall a time when you were at a concert, or a music performance, and felt it. Some even relate it to a "religious" experience. (And this is felt in all art, including visual art, photography, poetry, theater, etc.)

I can easily recall a moment, about six years ago when I went to see Sara Bareilles at The Anthem in Washington D.C. I was about halfway back on the floor. She had a great band and she, and they, sounded great as she went through some of her back catalog and new work. About halfway through, the band left the stage and Sara sat at the piano alone and sang "She Used to be Mine," a song that she wrote for the Broadway musical Waitress. In that moment, I had an aesthetic "religious" experience. First off, the song is amazing, sung by the lead character when she hits rock bottom, is lost, and mourning her lost former self. And Sara’s performance was nothing less than magical. The audience was completely silent, and totally at her command. It was one of the most amazing live music moments that I’ve ever experienced; while listening, I felt chills and became emotional, like many others I’m sure. I experienced the true power of music as connection in my mind, body, and soul.

And she had to feel that coming back to her, which had to add to her performance and experience of the music. You cannot get this from listening to recorded music.

However, as we continue to move through this Insta-TikTok-social media fueled world, what do you see at virtually every live music performance? People with their phones out, filming the concert, essentially watching and experiencing the performance, the art, through a screen. The "connection" is broken.

A live music experience should be a more pure form of aesthetic exchange where one is not trying to capture a moment but experience it. If you are going to try to experience a live music concert through your phone, why not just stay home and listen to the recording or watch a YouTube video? It’s much cheaper.

Music Therapy

Music therapy experiences in the hospital are all about connection. Connection between the therapist and the patient, the patient and the music, and the patient and themselves. In all of my experiences – from performer, to audience member, to now music therapist – this is the most "pure" form of aesthetic connection.

In a world of social media, the isolation of smartphones, and A.I., presence and human connection are needed more than ever, especially for someone who is in the hospital and challenged with a life-threatening illness.

Music is a great connector. We can communicate through music in a way that we cannot through words. Music transcends spoken language. Music expresses emotion and provides validation and empathy. And music creates an aesthetic connection, as it did with my patient in this example:

"He was in pain. Three weeks in the hospital with complications from brain surgery. He could only lie in bed and stare at the ceiling. A journey. A grind. When will it end? But now… something different. Something aesthetic. I offered some soundscape on the guitar. Something to help refocus, and ‘hold’ him in the space. After 30 minutes, as the music was winding down, I noticed that his face was ‘softer’. Then he said… 'The morning mist. That is what I’m seeing and feeling with the music. The morning mist.'"

So… the next time you go to a concert, experience it. Don’t try to ‘capture’ it. Experience it fully, with your mind, body, and soul. Live in the moment and create the memory. My memory of Sara Bareilles’s performance of "She Used to be Mine" is captured in my brain, and I will always have that memory. And when I recall that memory, I feel it all again.

The healing power of music…

item.title: This Is the Rarest Type of Intelligence
item.description:
Intelligence

This Is the Rarest Type of Intelligence

Why integrative intelligence, which goes way beyond IQ, is disappearing so fast.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Integrative intelligence is the ability to combine insights from unrelated fields to create new ideas.
  • Openness to experience is the personality trait most strongly linked to integrative intelligence.
  • Depth in multiple fields—not just broad knowledge—is essential for true integrative thinking.
Source: Ann H / Pexels

When psychologists talk about exceptional intelligence, the conversation almost always gravitates toward IQ. Our instinct to default to the measurable, scoreable, and rankable quantity is understandable.

However, decades of cognitive science have assembled a case for a different kind of mind entirely: one that doesn’t show up cleanly on standardized assessments, one that is incredibly difficult to cultivate, and one that may be more predictive of real-world creative impact than raw processing speed. Researchers sometimes call it integrative intelligence, and it’s the rare capacity to think fluently across unrelated domains and build something new at the intersections.

Why People Misunderstand This Intelligence

The first mistake people make is confusing integrative intelligence with being broadly knowledgeable. A well-read person might know the history of jazz, the basics of evolutionary biology and the principles of architectural design. While that’s admirable, it isn’t necessarily indicative of integrative intelligence.

To understand what integrative intelligence might really look like, you should consider what Charles Darwin actually did. He didn’t simply read widely across natural history. He recognized that the economic logic Thomas Malthus used to describe human population pressure — more organisms competing for finite resources — could explain the mechanism driving species change. He borrowed a framework from one domain and used it to unlock a puzzle in a completely different one. That transfer, that structural borrowing across what most people treated as separate intellectual territories, is precisely what integrative intelligence looks like in action.

Psychologists who study creativity consistently identify analogical reasoning, or the ability to recognize that a problem in one domain has already been solved, in a different form, somewhere else, as the engine underneath this kind of thinking. A 2025 study published in Thinking Skills and Creativity confirmed analogical reasoning as a core cognitive mechanism linking cross-domain thinking directly to creative output.

The scientist who sees a biological process as an algorithm, the architect who borrows from fluid dynamics, and the composer who builds harmonic structure the way a mathematician builds proofs are people for whom domain boundaries are porous in a way they simply aren’t for most minds.

The Personality Trait Most Closely Linked To Integrative Intelligence

Of the five major personality dimensions, research consistently finds that openness to experience has the strongest relationship to creative achievement across multiple fields. More recently, this finding was reinforced by a 2023 meta-analysis published in Personality and Individual Differences that synthesized data from 63 studies and more than 24,000 participants. People high in openness are drawn toward novelty, complexity, and ideas that resist easy categorization. They tolerate ambiguity, like sitting with an unresolved question across two different disciplines for months or years, without the discomfort that would push most people toward premature closure.

Think of the engineer who spends her evenings studying classical composition, not because it’s useful to her work, but because something about harmonic tension feels structurally related to a problem in signal processing she hasn’t been able to crack. That kind of restless cross-pollination, which looks eccentric from the outside, is often exactly how integrative insights get made.

What makes this rare is not the trait itself, which exists on a continuous spectrum, but its combination with other qualities that tend to pull in opposite directions: sustained depth, rigorous discipline, and the patience to develop genuine expertise in more than one area rather than skimming across the surface of many. Breadth without depth is curiosity. Breadth with depth is something considerably harder to build.

Why This Intelligence Is Becoming Rarer

At the very moment when our most complex problems — in medicine, in climate science, in artificial intelligence — demand people who can synthesize across disciplines, the incentive systems of education and professional life have moved sharply in the opposite direction.

Imagine a graduate student who enters a neuroscience program with a serious background in philosophy of mind and a genuine interest in computational modeling. She is likely to be told, at multiple points, to pick a lane. Her committee wants publications in peer-reviewed journals organized around established subfields. Her job market requires her to present a coherent, narrow research identity. The intellectual range that might, over a career, produce something genuinely new is treated, institutionally, as a liability rather than an asset.

Psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi’s research on creative individuals across fields, detailed in his 1996 book Creativity: Flow and the Psychology of Discovery and Invention, found that the most exceptional thinkers tend to hold what he described as complex personalities. Complex personalities, according to Csikszentmihalyi, housed pairs of traits that seem contradictory but coexist productively. Examples include discipline and playfulness, or intellectual humility as well as intellectual confidence, or even an enhanced capacibility to zoom in and out of problems at will. This kind of psychological complexity is not something that can be trained directly. It tends to emerge from a life organized around genuine curiosity rather than credential-seeking.
